sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Mamaqucha** ​(*mamaqucha*) — ‌Sea, Fishermen ‌· ​Mother sea ​— ​belongs to ​the Incan ​tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ​under ‌the domain ​"Sea, ‌Fishermen". The ​name means ‌"Mother ​sea"[^1].

**Mamaqucha** ​— Quechua ​*mama*, ​'mother', and ​*qucha*, ‌'lake, sea' ​— is ‌the ​Andean sea ‌as mother: ​mother ‌of fishes, ​horizon ‌of the ​Inca world, ​the ‌one great ‌power their ‌mountain ​religion never ​fully ‌mastered. Coastal ​peoples made ​offerings ‌where desert ​meets surf; ​the ‌Inca themselves ​met ‌her only ​late, and ​named ​her with ​the kinship ‌word ‌they gave ​the ‌earth.[^2]

PuniCodex ​records the ​canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**Mamaqucha** and ‌serves ‌its temple ​at ‌[its temple](https://punicodex.com/mamaqucha/). ​The displayed ​form ​is ASCII-equivalent ‌— a ​description ​computed from ​the ‌displayed form ​itself. The ​plain ​ASCII form ‌*mamaqucha* contains ​the ‌same letters: ​no ‌recovered diacritics ​or special ‌encoding ‌is claimed. ​The work ​here ​is consistent ​citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives for ​this ​name; **Mamaqucha** ​is ​a scholarly ​transliteration ‌of the ​reconstructed ​spoken form. ‌Etymologically the ​name ‌means "Mother ​sea"[^1].

‌The canonical ​spelling ​**Mamaqucha** matches ​the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. ‌The plain ​ASCII ‌form *mamaqucha* ​contains ‌the same ​letters, ‌so no ​lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding ​transition is ‌claimed. The ‌editorial ‌work is ​to ​fix one ‌reviewed ​reference spelling, ​preserve ‌capitalization and ​provenance, ​and keep ‌the ​original evidence ‌visible. ​The displayed ​form ​is ASCII-equivalent ​— ‌a description ‌computed ​from the ‌displayed ​form itself.

​The letter-by-letter ‌transformation ‌runs:

- **m** ‌→ ‌**M** — ​Same, ‌capitalized
- **a** ​→ ​**a** — ​Same
- ‌**m** → ​**m** ​— Same
- ​**a** ‌→ **a** ​— ​Same
- **q** ​→ ‌**q** — ​Same
- ‌**u** → ​**u** — ‌Same
- ​**c** → ‌**c** ‌— Same
- ​**h** ​→ **h** ​— ​Same
- **a** ‌→ ‌**a** — ​Same

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/mamaqucha/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**mamaqucha** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Mamaqucha.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Mamaqucha" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Mamaqucha" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"mamaqucha" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Mamaqucha ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Mamaqucha ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Mamaqucha ‌place ​sea, fishermen ​at ​the ​center of ​a ‌living ​mythological world.

### ​Origins ‌(Myth)

​Mamaqucha appears ‌in ​incan ‌tradition as ​sea, ​fishermen. ​The name's ​meaning, ​"Mother ‌sea", shapes ​the ‌narratives ​told about ‌this ​figure.

### ‌Worship and ​Memory ‌(Cult)

​Devotees and ​later ‌tradition-keepers ‌preserved Mamaqucha ‌in ​ritual, ​text, and ‌iconography, ​ensuring ​the name ‌survived ​into ​the modern ‌scholarly ​record.

The ‌myths ​of ​Mamaqucha survive ​in ​fragments, ‌summaries, and ‌later ​retellings. ‌Each version ​reflects ​the ‌interests of ‌its ‌tellers ‌— poets, ​priests, ‌philosophers, ​and scholars. ​The ​PuniCodex ‌entry does ​not ​privilege ​a single ‌version; ​it ​gathers the ​attestations ‌so ​that readers ‌can ​compare ‌them. The ​restoration ‌Mamaqucha ‌gives the ​figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Mamaqucha ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Incan ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Mamaqucha, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​sea ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: The ​Andes are ‌a ‌vertical civilization: ​it ​reads the ​world ​up and ​down ‌— terraces, ​peaks, ​apus above, ‌dead ​below. Mamaqucha ‌is ​the great ‌exception, ​the horizontal. ​Where ​every apu ​is ​a named, ‌ranked, ​assigned lord, ‌the ​sea is ‌simply ​Mother — ‌an ​address, not ‌an ​inventory entry. ​That ‌asymmetry is ‌the ‌whole theology. ​The ​state could ‌measure ​a mountain ​into ‌its ritual ​circuit; ​it could ‌not ​measure an ‌ocean, ​and so ​it ​left the ​ocean ‌in the ‌one ​grammatical case ‌it ​could not ​administer: ‌the vocative. ‌To ‌call the ‌sea ​'mother' is ‌to ​admit that ​some ​powers are ‌fed ​by being ​spoken ​to, not ‌by ​being organized. ​This ​temple keeps ‌that ​admission. Mamaqucha ‌is ​the entry ‌in ​the lexicon ‌that ‌refused to ​become ​a monument, ​and ​is honored ‌precisely ‌for the ​refusal.[^1]
